name: Romana Kuts
body:
I got sick for a few days recently, came back to LinkedIn, and half my feed had apparently mastered Claude, built entire automated systems, and shipped more in a week than I had in a month.

My first reaction was to think everyone else knew something I had missed.

But I think this is the most honest thing I can say about our industry right now:

"We're all figuring this out in real time"

The pace right now is moving fast enough that experience only gives you pattern recognition.

5 or 25 years of B2B content experience doesn't mean I automatically know the right AI workflow better than someone six months into their career who happened to experiment with the right tool last week.

That might be uncomfortable thing to admit publicly when your actual job title has 'expert' baked into how people perceive you.

But I think pretending otherwise is worse, because it teaches everyone watching that falling behind for a week means you've permanently lost ground, when in reality, things change so fast that the gap starts closing as soon as you sit down and try.

My actual advice, the same thing I tell people I mentor: get a 20$ Claude subscription and build something for yourself first, before trying to formalize a workflow for a client.

Because the only way pattern recognition actually forms is by building the pattern yourself, and no amount of watching someone else's LinkedIn post about their system gives you that the same way actually doing it does. Period.

I've also started saying this openly to clients too.

When someone asks whether our team has fully mastered a specific new AI workflow, the honest answer is usually that we're testing it in real time alongside them, and I would rather be transparent about that than perform a confidence that isn't real.

Clients respond better to this as well because most of them are also living the similar uncertainty internally, and hearing an agency admit it plainly seems to build more trust, not less.

name: Romana Kuts
body:
We started doing something with client blog content that looked unnecessary the first time I suggested it.

- Embedding a 3 min Loom video under the H1, with a subject matter expert simply answering the core question of the article on camera, before a single paragraph of text.

I get why most people would skip this - it's extra production work for an asset most assume nobody will watch, competing against a reader who just wants to skim the article and leave.

And I would have agreed two years ago. But watching the engagement and time-on-page data for articles that had the video vs the ones that didn't, across enough client accounts, it stopped looking like a coincidence.

Here's my actual read on why it works, beyond the raw numbers: A video from a real subject matter expert proves that a real person who actually knows this topic is behind the content, rather than a generic byline attached to something that could have been assembled from other people's articles.

In a search landscape where AI-generated content is flooding every category at volume, that proof of an actual human perspective is becoming one of the only differentiators left that's genuinely hard to fake convincingly.

It's also, honestly, not that expensive to produce once you build the habit. A subject matter expert doesn't need a script or a production crew. All they need is one simple question to answer in their own words, imperfections and all.

I'd rather ship a slightly rough video that proves a real person is behind the content than a flawlessly polished paragraph that could have come from anyone, anywhere, about almost anything.

We've made this a normal part of how we create content when a client has a subject matter expert.

It doesn't work for every piece, and I don't think it should. But for the pieces where a genuine POV matters, having a real person say it on camera has become one of the more reliably effective additions to our own playbook.

name: Romana Kuts
body:
B2B content was already bad before AI came along.

I'll say that as plainly as I said it the first time, because it's the actual root of the problem everyone's currently blaming on AI.

Walk through 10 blogs in any category and count how many of them say anything a competitor couldn't have said with the names swapped.

Before ChatGPT/Claude existed, that content was already generic, already optimized for a keyword instead of a reader, already written by someone with zero actual conversations with the buyer.

AI just made it possible to produce the same generic content at 10x the volume, which is a considerably worse outcome.

I've led content teams at Leadfeeder and Dealfront - I've seen this pattern up close: the blog posts that drove pipeline were the ones written from an actual, specific POV, usually pulled directly from a real sales call, a real customer objection, a real internal debate about how to position something.

What AI has actually done, and this part gets missed in most of the panic, is remove the excuse.

It used to be genuinely expensive and slow to produce a lot of mediocre content, so mediocre content at least had scarcity working in its favor. But now mediocre content is nearly free to produce at scale, which means the only thing left to differentiate on is whether it was actually worth writing in the first place.

That's a harder standard to hold yourself to than a word count or a keyword density target, and in my opinion it's the standard B2B content should have been held to all along.

Every time a prospective client asks what makes SaaStorm different from the last agency they tried, the answer is we still hold every piece we ship to the same question a good editor would have asked before AI ever existed: does this actually deserve a reader's attention, or does it just fill a slot on the calendar. That question is always the right filter. It always has been.

name: Romana Kuts
body:
Every new engagement at our agency SaaStorm starts with a 2-week discovery phase with no strings.

And at the end of it, a prospective client can choose to partner with us, or take the results and run with them entirely on their own.

We get asked fairly often why we'd structure things this way.

The answer is that we think it's the only fair test of whether a revenue-focused marketing claim actually holds up under scrutiny.

It's easy for any agency to promise results in a sales conversation. It's a considerably higher bar to deliver something genuinely useful in the first 2 weeks, before any long-term commitment exists to soften the standard we're holding ourselves to.

We've had prospective clients take those 2 weeks of work and go execute it themselves, without ever becoming a paying client. We've made peace with that as an acceptable outcome of the model instead of a failure of it.

If 2 weeks of work convinces a team they don't need us, that's a more genuine signal than a longer sales cycle built on promises instead of delivered work would've given either of us.

What this structure actually protects, more than anything, is the quality of the engagements that do convert.

A client who partners with us after seeing useful work firsthand, instead of after being sold on a pitch deck, tends to have realistic expectations about what we can actually deliver.

Makes for a considerably healthier working relationship over the following months than one built on a promise that hasn't yet been tested against output.

We've had a few internal debates about whether giving away 2 weeks of work for free is too generous a model to sustain at scale.

So far, the conversion quality from prospects who've seen output first has more than justified the occasional walk-away. And we'd rather protect that quality than chase a slightly higher close rate built on less proof upfront.
